articles.title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
articles.full_content:
A memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. A remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, read it in the style of Heartbleed, and reach remote code execution.

After we disclosed PHP2Shell, we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java.

Today, we are disclosing Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the most popular Java runtime. Under CVSS 4.0, this vulnerability scores 9.2 out of 10 (CRITICAL).

While PHP is a high-level web technology, Java sits much deeper. Java is the world's third most popular programming language, powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies. It is the beating heart of the modern economy. Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems.

Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages. To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:

In older OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 128 of A followed by =.

Write once, RCE everywhere

Our initial testing demonstrated remote code execution in the following widely deployed Java applications, in their default configs.

Pre-auth RCE:

Keycloak

Atlassian Jira

Atlassian Confluence

JFrog Artifactory

Jenkins

PingFederate

Post-auth RCE:

Apache Kafka Broker

Apache Solr

Elasticsearch

Gerrit

Spinnaker

The lists are non-exhaustive. We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested. samczsun also shared a client-side exploit with us. A Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own.

Here are a demo video of the exploits running:

Wait, Java has a memory-corruption vulnerability, in Base64?!

Yes. First time?

Memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the Internet. But one of Java's biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers' behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software.

But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life.

To speed up Base64 decoding, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors. The bug sits in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters. For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array. After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array. Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted.

Era of the centaur hacker

As with PHP2Shell, Calif used AI to find and weaponize Java4Shell. AI brings the horsepower. Our researchers bring the context. The best hacker today is neither AI nor human. It is the centaur hacker, part human, part AI.

It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit. The total token cost was less than $200.

One thing to note about this vulnerability is that there is no universal exploit. Depending on how Base64 is used and how the application works, different steps may be required for exploitation. Calif was able to accelerate the exploit development by spending initial effort building pipelines and strategies, then directing AI agents to use those for initial exploitation. Afterwards, most of the later chains are built almost autonomously with AI.

The tragedy of the commons

Java is one of many shared software stacks we all rely on. Over the years, it has grown to serve many different needs. Each feature request may make sense on its own, but everyone inherits the added complexity. Those who need a feature get the benefit. Everyone else carries the code and its risks, even if they never use it.

Java4Shell is a concrete example. The Base64 optimization helps applications that decode enormous amounts of data. But the code ships to everyone else too, including applications that gain little from it. On affected systems, an optimization few applications needed became a serious security risk.

Features can be useful, and most bugs can be fixed. But why do we have to worry about code we never needed in the first place?

A call for vibe-uncoding

If you don't need something, there is little reason to keep it running in your systems. Do you need that hand-rolled assembly Base64 decoder to process a few hundred bytes? Probably not.

Earlier this year we found Squidbleed, an older cousin of Heartbleed, hiding in the Squid proxy since 1997. The bug was in Squid's FTP module. But who uses FTP anymore? It's a dead protocol and should be removed.

Removing code is harder than it sounds. An apparently unused feature may have hidden dependencies. Someone has to understand what can be removed, make the change, and test what remains.

This is where AI can help to make that work practical at a scale we could not previously afford.

The same centaur hacker that discovered PHP2Shell and Java4Shell can comb a large codebase and flag dead code, bloated features, and needless optimizations. We call this vibe-uncoding: identify the parts a system actually needs, then remove everything else to reduce its attack surface.

With AI, everyone is asking, “What can we build?” But maybe the right question for security is, “What can we delete?”

The Tail of Base64

By Quang Luong

On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution.

Discovery

A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode.

After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into some thing completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway.

Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues.

Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder...

Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold?

The vulnerability

The issue lies in OpenJDK HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. C2 is the most aggressive JIT compiler in the Java Virtual Machine. Specifically, if you trigger a function repeatedly, then it will compile that function into native code. Even then, ordinary native code itself is not fast enough. Modern CPUs have specialized instructions that allow processing data even faster. HotSpot uses them in optimized routines called intrinsics. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write.

The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic iterates through the input in 256-byte blocks; if it is less than 256, then it will do so in 64-byte blocks. When the input is less than 64 bytes, it uses evmovdqub, the intrinsic for the VMOVDQU8 instruction. This instruction takes a 64-bit mask that decides which bytes are read from or written to memory. The mask is first calculated from the input and output length, then updated to reflect the number of padding bytes ('=') in the Base64-encoded string. This is shown in the following (pseudocode):

// Zero High Bits Starting with Specified Bit Position input_mask := bzhiq(-1, input_length) output_len := (input_length / 4) * 3 // handle padding if input[input_length - 1] == '=': output_len -= 1 input_mask >>= 1 if input[input_length - 2] == '=': output_len -= 1 input_mask >>= 1 output_mask := bzhiq(-1, output_len)

In the above code, if the remaining input is of the form =, ==, X=, X==, XY=, or ===, then output_len will be computed as zero. However, since there is padding, output_len is decremented, resulting in an underflowed value of -1 or -2. Since bzhiq(-1, output_len) doesn’t change any bits if output_len >= 64, this results in output_mask == -1u64.

Later the code uses evmovdqub to read and write multiple bytes at a time. For a write, if the mask bit is 1, the byte at that index in the vector register is written to memory. So when output_mask == -1u64, all 64 bytes are written during the following operation:

The generated stub returns the number of bytes it successfully decoded, and returns early when it detects invalid input. The remaining bytes are handled by the Java code, which throws IllegalArgumentException if the input is invalid.

At runtime, the decoded buffer length is calculated as (ceil(inp_len / 4) * 3) - padding. When the bug is triggered, with 65 bytes ([64 bytes] + '=') as input, that calculation allocates a 50-byte buffer. During decoding the bug makes output_mask == -1 for evmovdqub, so 64 bytes are written starting at offset 48, an out-of-bounds write past the end of the buffer.

On OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 'A' * 128 + '=' instead of 'A' * 64 + '=', because the length threshold to reach the code path is higher.

Exploitation strategy

The Base64 bug was gold, but not the type that sits on the riverbed waiting to be panned out. It was the type that was deep, dark, and hard to access. While we had memory corruption, exploiting it looked difficult, perhaps even borderline unexploitable, since it only wrote fixed bytes to the heap. Only the landing position of the out-of-bounds write is controllable.

We get the following 64 bytes write starting from the position in buffer where the remaining sets of Base64 decoded bytes would have been written to:

Full controlled write to byte 0 (in bound)

4-bit controlled write to byte 1 (in bound)

Uncontrolled write to bytes [2, 63]. For bytes 48..63, the value will always be 0x9a.

The uncontrolled out-of-bounds write turned out not to be a big problem. We reused a common JavaScript engine exploitation primitive, the classic technique of overwriting a buffer length.

We call the buffer whose length we overwrite the writer. Once its length is corrupted, it keeps accepting our chosen bytes, so if we place another array or object after it, we can corrupt that neighbor with all of our chosen values. That upgrades the fixed write into a bounded, chosen-value linear write.

If we then corrupt another array's length and its data is copied back into the response, we have built a heap disclosure primitive, the reader, from the out-of-bounds read. At this point, before any code execution, we already had JavaBleed, the ability to leak contents from the Java heap, which may hold PII, private keys, other secret keys, and tokens.

From the writer and reader, the rest of this write-up builds the full attack. We repair the objects the linear write damaged to keep the JVM running, mount data-only attacks on application logic, and escalate the bounded write into arbitrary writes that reach the Code Cache and JVM hooks for code execution.

But first things first, we need to align the heap to our advantage.

HotSpot normally gives each Java thread a thread-local allocation buffer (TLAB), a private slice of Eden. Objects created by different request threads advance different cursors, which gives us no useful order between a Base64 decoder in one TLAB and a writer in another.

The first grooming layer controls the allocation route. The critical array's size and the space left in the worker's TLAB decide whether HotSpot refills that TLAB or takes the attacker-preferred outside-TLAB allocation path.

The second layer controls the layout. However, we do not choose how G1 allocates memory, and we don't know the current heap state. To approach this limitation, Calif used the tried and tested method of Spray and Pray.

Object sizes and padding fix offsets inside region-sized spans. We spray several live writer and reader pairs to give the decoder output several possible neighbors. When its region lands immediately below a writer region, the widened reader produces a larger application response. We discard misses and retry until successful.

One early challenge during exploit development was that the AI would get stuck during heap grooming primitive development. In order to save tokens and time, Calif wrote a small heap tracer and visualizer to give the agent information about the heap state, combined with our expertise on specific cases.

Remote Heap Feng Shui

In order to perform remote grooming, each request data would be sent up until the critical heap allocation would occur. By ensuring the data that was previously sent had a TCP acknowledgement, the exploit would have control over the allocations up to date. Once we were confident our data so far is buffered on the target, we then sent the rest, completing the http request. This allows both heap allocation control and more precise schedule as delivering small network packets is more stable than big ones.

The exact allocation and free order schedule belongs to the targeted application profile, while we are able to control the adding, writer, reader, and decoder pieces.

The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.

Warm-up, rehearsal, and retries

To summarize the chain so far, we will warm up the Base64 decoder to C2 tier. We can rehearse the exploit run to calibrate timing and responses against the target before causing corruption to occur. Once the required information has been obtained, we can trigger the vulnerability. Incorrect placement could cause the JVM to crash, but in many instances, we can simply try again.

WARM

Run valid decodes until the JIT selects the affected fast path. No memory is corrupted.

REHEARSE

Optional safe round for calibration.

TRIGGER

Send the malformed tail. If the objects line up, the fixed spill enlarges the writer.

DISCLOSE

Continue the writer so chosen bytes enlarge the reader, then collect the response-derived heap bytes.

REPAIR

Use the disclosed originals to restore temporary headers and untouched neighbors when the chain has a repair path.

FINISH

Make the application-specific change and verify it through a live request.

Limitations

Request streaming. Some current grooming profiles need partial request bodies to reach the application. A proxy that waits for the complete body removes their release timing. nginx buffers request bodies by default.

Request buffering is not a general mitigation. Elasticsearch runs from one complete request, so this setting does not stop that chain. After a configured WebSocket upgrade, later frames pass through a tunnel and request-body buffering no longer applies to them.

Application profiles. There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot.

PoC

Here is a self-contained proof of concept. It warms the Base64 decoder until the vulnerable intrinsic is used, then decodes the malformed 64 × "A" + "=" input into a 4096-byte array. On an affected JDK it prints REPRODUCED: the decoder rejects the input, but 62 bytes (offsets 50 to 111) past the decoded output have already been overwritten. Every write lands inside a real array, so the trigger is safe to run.

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.Base64; /** Bounded standalone trigger: every write stays inside a real 4096-byte array. */ public final class Base64Trigger { private static volatile int sink; public static void main(String[] args) { Base64.Decoder decoder = Base64.getDecoder(); byte[] valid = "A".repeat(64).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII); byte[] malformed = ("A".repeat(64) + "=").getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII); byte[] target = new byte[4096]; for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) { sink += decoder.decode(valid, target); } Arrays.fill(target, (byte) 0x5a); boolean rejected = false; try { decoder.decode(malformed, target); } catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) { rejected = true; } int changed = 0; int first = -1; int last = -1; for (int i = 50; i < target.length; i++) { if (target[i] != (byte) 0x5a) { changed++; if (first < 0) first = i; last = i; } } System.out.println("runtime=" + System.getProperty("java.runtime.version")); System.out.println("vm=" + System.getProperty("java.vm.name")); System.out.printf("rejected=%s changed=%d first=%d last=%d%n", rejected, changed, first, last); if (!rejected || changed != 62 || first != 50 || last != 111) { System.err.println("NOT REPRODUCED"); System.exit(1); } System.out.println("REPRODUCED"); } }

We are holding back the application-specific exploits for now. This write-up covers the vulnerability and the general exploitation technique. The weaponized chains for individual products stay private until everyone has had a chance to upgrade. We will publish them later.

Affected products

Java4Shell affects OpenJDK from version 17.0.6 or newer.

Because they are built from OpenJDK, the following Java distributions are also vulnerable:

Amazon Corretto

Eclipse Temurin

Microsoft Build of OpenJDK

Azul Zulu

BellSoft Liberica

SAP SapMachine

Red Hat OpenJDK

Oracle OpenJDK

Oracle Java SE

Oracle GraalVM for JDK

According to Oracle, the following Oracle Java SE versions are vulnerable: 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3. We thank Oracle for providing this information ahead of publication time.

Because the vulnerable code is hardware-specific, Java4Shell also requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support. ARM64 CPUs are not affected.

These mainstream CPU families meet the hardware requirements:

Intel Xeon: Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids

AMD EPYC and Ryzen: Zen 4 or newer

articles.title: Quad9's withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
articles.full_content:
Quad9’s withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine

Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement.

Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable. The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users. Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead.

The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet. It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives. Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France — including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities — and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working. If the affected parties do not change their resolver before Quad9 removes its service, their Internet will fail with no explanation.

Quad9 is not the first public DNS resolver to withdraw from a country following blocking orders, and it almost certainly won’t be the last. Cisco previously withdrew its OpenDNS resolver from France, Portugal, and Belgium (temporarily) under similar circumstances. And a Belgian court recently issued an order that would impose substantial penalties if Cloudflare, Google, and Cisco do not begin blocking websites through their public resolvers by early January 2027. That’s something Cloudflare has never done.

Cloudflare has spent years advocating against orders of this kind. We are concerned that rightsholders’ unrelenting demands for blocking by public DNS resolvers will end up causing real harm to the Internet.

A refresher on DNS, the Domain Name System

To understand why this is such a problem, it helps to understand how the Internet works under the hood. DNS resolvers are a foundational piece of the Internet’s infrastructure. DNS is the Internet’s address book: when you type a website name such as cloudflare.com, the DNS system translates that domain name into the IP address your device needs to connect to it. A DNS resolver is the service that looks up that address and sends it back to your device, much like an operator finding a phone number in a directory.

DNS resolvers can be operated by anyone, but they are commonly run by Internet service providers (ISPs), mobile networks, businesses, and universities. If you’re reading this blog post at home and have never thought about DNS before, chances are that you’re using your ISP’s default resolver. Because you use your DNS resolver every time that you visit a website, it’s important for it to be reliable and trustworthy.

And because the DNS resolver has access to all of your browsing activity, which resolver you use has real privacy implications.

In addition to DNS resolvers that are provided by your local ISP, there are a variety of public DNS resolvers available. Cloudflare launched our public DNS resolver 1.1.1.1 in April 2018 to give back to the Internet. Our goal was to make a fast, reliable, privacy-first consumer DNS service available for free to everyone. We succeeded. 1.1.1.1 is among the fastest DNS resolvers in the world, including in Europe. Cloudflare's resolver doesn’t collect any user data, let alone sell it to advertisers. 1.1.1.1 has always been one of our favorite examples of Cloudflare fulfilling its mission to help build a better Internet.

1.1.1.1 is one of many public resolvers that anyone can use. In addition to 1.1.1.1 and Quad9’s 9.9.9.9, some of the other best-known public resolvers include Google’s 8.8.8.8 and Cisco’s OpenDNS. Just because these services are offered for free doesn’t mean they’re easy to provide. A well-run global public DNS resolver is an extraordinary engineering feat, built to securely and privately resolve hundreds of billions or even trillions of queries a day across a globally distributed network of hundreds of server locations.

As Quad9 notes, there are many other DNS resolvers available to users, many of them offered by essentially anonymous services whose practices are unknown or undocumented. It’s easy to change your DNS resolver, and people do so for a variety of reasons including performance, reliability, or to access specific security features.

Why public DNS resolvers should not be required to block

Rightsholders have a legitimate interest in preventing online piracy. But trying to address online infringement through public DNS resolvers is fundamentally the wrong approach.

Among other things, such blocking is ineffective. Think back to the analogy of an operator finding a phone number in a directory. If a court wants to shut down an illegal business, forcing the directory operator to cross the business's name out of the phone book doesn't actually close the business. The storefront is still open, the products are still there, and anyone who already knows the address, or uses a different phone book, can walk in.

The same is true for the Internet. DNS resolvers are just one link in the transmission chain. The only way a DNS resolver can “block” content is by declining to return the IP address for a particular website. But a public DNS resolver cannot remove the actual infringing content from the Internet, nor can it take down the servers hosting it.

Because of this, blocking by public DNS resolvers is remarkably easy to bypass. Any Internet user who wants to reach a blocked site can circumvent the block in less than a minute simply by switching to one of the thousands of other DNS resolvers available online. In fact, users don’t even need a resolver at all to reach infringing content if they already know the underlying IP address. Unsurprisingly, while blocking via public resolvers may inject some friction for some users when accessing content, there is no evidence that it actually reduces the total amount of online infringement that occurs.

In addition to being ineffective, as we’ve written previously, DNS blocking is a blunt instrument that causes collateral damage. Because DNS operates at the domain level, a resolver cannot block a specific infringing video or file; it must block the entire domain. This affects all content on that domain, whether legal or illegal. It is also entirely opaque to the user: when a resolver is forced to block a domain, the website simply fails to load. The user receives no explanation or legal notice, making it impossible to know if the site is down for maintenance, if their network is broken, or if the site was blocked by a court order.

The problem is substantially worse with respect to public DNS resolvers. Because public resolvers operate globally, any blocking will naturally cross borders, meaning that a single country could dictate what content is accessible around the world. For example, while the EU-dedicated DNS resolver DNS4EU operated by Whalebone blocks in response to country-specific orders, it does so across the entire EU. Efforts to reengineer public DNS resolvers to allow for more localized blocking would fundamentally alter the service, harming performance and resilience, undermining user privacy, and fragmenting the open Internet.

For these reasons, Cloudflare, Google, Cisco, and Quad9 have all opposed efforts to mandate blocking by public DNS resolvers, with some success. Several years ago, courts in Germany ruled in favor of Cloudflare and Quad9, rejecting requests to require DNS blocking. More recently, a French court rejected penalties against Cloudflare for failing to block through 1.1.1.1, finding that other actions we had taken through our CDN and reverse-proxy service were sufficient to comply with the underlying order.

Undeterred, rightsholders have continued to press for blocking by public resolvers with a level of determination that is hard to explain. A recent study found that the majority of online piracy in Europe is hosted in Europe. If rightsholders want to genuinely address online infringement, there are far better places to focus their efforts — most notably by requiring the hosting providers who actually store the pirated files to take them down.

Forcing public DNS resolvers out of markets hurts the Internet

The French court’s penalty order against Quad9 represents the culmination of these rightsholder efforts. As a small non-profit that only offers a public DNS resolver, Quad9 had no alternative methods for demonstrating compliance with the order. The French court therefore granted rightsholders’ request to issue penalties for non-compliance, forcing Quad9 to undermine its own service or leave the country.

Quad9’s withdrawal from France represents a genuine loss for the Internet. In the short term, removal of Quad9’s resolver is likely to cause immediate and potentially severe disruptions to Internet access. Because of the way their service is set up to preserve privacy, Quad9 has no way to know who exactly is using its resolver, let alone to directly communicate to them about the upcoming withdrawal of services. That means that individuals, hospitals, universities, and government offices all may be caught unaware when the resolver stops working. Again, because of how DNS resolvers work, those users will not receive a detailed error message explaining what happened — their Internet will simply stop working. The problem will be even worse when devices like security systems or thermostats are hardwired to use Quad9’s resolver. Fixing these issues may be slow or even impossible.

More generally, driving Quad9 out of France does absolutely nothing to prevent online infringement, but it does leave everyday Internet users with fewer safe, reliable options, particularly ones like Quad9 that also protect users from phishing and malware. Taking established public DNS resolvers away forces Internet users to fall back on the default resolvers offered by their ISPs (which may monetize their browsing data), try lesser-known resolvers operated by anonymous or less trustworthy organizations, or run their own resolver. The irony is that Quad9 and Cloudflare are being pulled into court precisely because we are transparent, reputable organizations. Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web.

The way forward

If nothing else, we hope that Quad9’s announcement may serve as a wake-up call to rightsholders and policymakers that seeking to block infringement at every layer of the Internet has real costs.

We believe there are far better ways to work together to fight piracy without compromising the integrity of the Internet, and Cloudflare continues to pursue innovative collaborations to that end. Our collective efforts in addressing online infringement would be put to better use in seeking to have such content removed at the hosting provider, which would both achieve a more durable solution and avoid collateral damage to the Internet.

In the meantime, we will keep resisting misguided efforts to require blocking by public DNS resolvers. Along with Google and Cisco, we have appealed the Belgian order that would impose penalties on us if we do not start DNS blocking by January 2027. We hope to get a resolution before the end of the year that would avoid another situation like the one Quad9 faces now in France.

We have grave concerns about the disruption that would be caused if additional resolvers are forced to withdraw from markets, and we will continue to advocate against that possible result.

articles.title: Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%
articles.full_content:
Google's AI Overviews cut clicks to websites by 40%

Google's AI answers are taking clicks from websites in the search results. In a randomized experiment, researchers hid AI Overviews from some US desktop users. Comparing them with users who still saw Overviews shows that an Overview cuts clicks to outside websites by about 40%. Those Overviews now appear on more than half the US keywords DataForSEO tracks, up from 6% two years ago. The industry's answer, GEO (generative engine optimization), has yet to show a way to compensate for the loss. While AI citations correlate with the same kind of link profile that goes with higher Google rankings, in March AI assistants sent websites just 0.3% of their traffic.

Search engine optimization (SEO) still decides whether you can be found, but where an AI answer appears, a ranking brings 40% fewer visits than it used to. Generative engine optimization (GEO), the practice of getting your content cited in AI-written answers, looks mostly like SEO plus two additions: being present on the third-party sites AI answers draw from, and writing pages that are easy to quote. We found little evidence for any other tactic.

Google answers first

An AI Overview is a generated summary that Google places above the ordinary results, with links to the pages it drew on. In DataForSEO's monthly panel of 20 million keywords, the share of results showing one climbed from 5.93% in September 2024 to 61.43% in August 2026. The chart at the top of this post shows that climb. Over the same period the featured snippet, the quoted passage Google used to show at the top of a page, fell from 8.96% to 0.44%, and the discussions and forums block fell from 21.13% to 7.42%. Video results rose from 9.67% to 19.98%, though that is down from a peak of 31.05% in October 2025, and local map listings rose from 19.98% to 25.99%. DataForSEO's dataset covers 190 million keywords, 165 million AI answers, and 1.1 billion backlinks, mostly for US English searches. Pew Research Center's data gives an independent check. Pew logged the searches of 900 US adults in March 2025, re-ran them in April, and found summaries on 18% of them. DataForSEO's figures for those months are 14.67% and 17.63%, close to Pew's.

You can't reliably avoid Overviews by choosing different keywords. Between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026, the rate rose for every type of search intent:

Search intentQ4 2025Q3 2026
Informational (looking something up)48.42%70.44%
Commercial (comparing options)26.30%51.35%
Navigational (looking for a site)17.04%34.03%
Transactional (ready to buy)10.82%28.64%

Low-volume keywords aren't safer either. In the third quarter of 2026, keywords with 201 to 300 monthly searches showed Overviews 58.59% of the time, against 48.62% for those above 600. A separate dataset, from June to September 2026, covers difficulty and price. The easiest keywords showed Overviews 60.64% of the time and the hardest 53.76%. Keywords costing advertisers more than $5 a click were at 49.55% and those under 25 cents at 50.54%, with a low of 42.63% between $0.51 and $1.00. More than half the result pages have no price data and show Overviews 60.06% of the time. The rate does vary by industry. Health is at 69.68% and finance at 68.80%, while apparel is at 37.48%, dining at 29.37%, and real estate at 22.27%.

Queries are also getting longer, especially on desktop. Over a year, queries of five or more words grew from 29.3% to 34.8% of unique desktop queries and from 29.6% to 31.9% on mobile. Three and four word searches are still the most common.

What happens to the clicks

The strongest evidence is an experiment. Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen gave US desktop Chrome users an extension that put each of them at random into a group. One group saw Google as usual, and another had AI Overviews hidden. The researchers then watched two weeks of real searches in January and February 2026. On searches that would show an Overview, the group that could see them averaged 0.37 clicks to outside websites per search, against 0.62 for the group that couldn't, which the authors report as a 39.8% reduction. Searches ending with no outbound click went from 54% to 73%. Clicks on ads didn't change, which suggests Google takes care not to cannibalize its own revenue. Across all searches, with and without an Overview, the authors put the loss at roughly 18.5% of the organic clicks a site gets from Google. The authors expect the loss to grow as Overviews appear on more searches. This is a randomized controlled trial, the most reliable kind of study for separating cause from correlation or coincidence. The effect was statistically significant for informational searches. The navigational and transactional samples were too small to settle anything. This is a working paper, not yet peer reviewed, and it covers desktop only. A separate preregistered experiment by Wang and colleagues, with 1,100 people, also found that removing AI Overviews and AI Mode raised clicks to publishers.

Observational data points the same way. Pew found people clicked an ordinary result on 8% of visits to a results page with a summary and on 15% without one, and ended their browsing session on 26% against 16%. Pew's comparison isn't a controlled experiment, because the searches that draw a summary tend to be longer and phrased as questions.

Click-through rate (CTR) is the share of people shown a result who click it. Across more than 2,000 websites in DataForSEO's panel, the desktop CTR of the first organic result fell from 17.83% in September 2025 to 7.43% in August 2026, a drop of 58%. Mobile fell from 25.17% to 20.80%, a drop of 17%.

Desktop plunged from 15.18% to 7.94% between February and March 2026. AI Overviews can't easily explain that step since the report has them almost flat that month, at 42.79% and then 43.38%. A change in the format or quality of the Overviews might explain part of it, though that is speculation on our part. Mobile, meanwhile, sank to 12.96% and then rebounded to 22.49% by May. The report itself says its data "does not establish" whether AI answers, layout changes, or changes in behavior are the cause. Its sample may also be shifting underneath it, since the unique desktop queries it counts fell by a third over the year, from 1.97 million to 1.32 million. Whatever the cause, a top ranking on desktop now earns less than half the clicks it did a year earlier.

DataForSEO also estimates where clicks go on pages with and without an Overview. By its model, the first organic result holds 9 to 16 points less click share on pages with one, though these are different searches on a single day's snapshot:

Search intentPosition 1, no OverviewPosition 1, with OverviewOverview's cited links
Informational37.1%20.7%42.4%
Navigational33.4%24.1%44.8%
Transactional37.6%21.4%43.0%
Commercial33.8%21.1%42.2%

The click share for the Overview's cited links looks promising, but it comes from a model. Pew, which logged real browsing, saw people click a link inside a summary on just 1% of visits, against 8% for ordinary results. Eighteen months and a large change in the product separate the two measurements, so it is difficult to say which is closer to the truth.

Google disputes that search traffic to websites is declining. In August 2025 its head of Search, Liz Reid, wrote that total organic clicks were "relatively stable year-over-year" and that Google was sending "slightly more quality clicks", meaning clicks where people don't quickly come back. She gave no figures to back that up.

Your site can't see whether someone goes back to Google, so you can't check Google's quality-clicks claim yourself, but you can check what your Google clicks are worth. RevScope, our product, shows your revenue per visitor from Google, AI Overviews included, and which landing pages earn the most.

Who the answers cite

If people read the summary and stop there, it matters which sites the summary cites. The report compares Google's AI Overviews with ChatGPT. Their most-cited lists overlap, but a different kind of site leads each one.

RankGoogle AI OverviewsCitationsChatGPTAnswers citing it
1youtube.com51.9Mwikipedia.org4.88M
2reddit.com25.1Mreddit.com3.25M
3facebook.com20.4Mfandom.com670K
4wikipedia.org19.9Mbritannica.com486K
5google.com15.9Mnih.gov476K

The report warns that the two platforms' counts aren't comparable, so compare where a site ranks within each list. Reddit and Wikipedia rank near the top of both, and by our count 16 of the 30 domains in each top 30 appear on both lists. The differences are still large. YouTube is first in AI Overviews and nineteenth in ChatGPT. Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok make Google's top ten and miss ChatGPT's top 30, while Reuters, The Guardian, AP News, and The Washington Post make ChatGPT's top 30 and miss Google's. ChatGPT also often cites nobody: 27.3% of its answers had no source, against 0.7% for AI Overviews. So, as the report puts it, strength on one platform "doesn't automatically guarantee" the same on another.

Reddit also appears in Google's ordinary top ten for 32.15% of the report's tracked results, nearly eight times Quora's 4.11%. Two limits apply to all of this. The first is that the answers come from prompts DataForSEO collected, and the report doesn't explain how they were chosen or whether they match what people really ask. The second is that big platforms do about as well in ordinary results: Pew found Wikipedia, YouTube, and Reddit made up 15% of the sources in AI summaries and 17% of those in standard results. Still, the common belief that AI favors Reddit holds up in this data.

GEO looks mostly like SEO

Google's position is that there are "no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary", beyond a page being indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. Since that is a company describing its own product, we looked at outside data on two questions. The first is which sites get considered, and the second is which page on a site gets picked.

Which sites: link profiles correlate with citations

A referring domain is another website that links to yours. DataForSEO measured how closely referring domains track AI citations using Spearman's correlation, a score where 0 means no relationship between two rankings and 1 means they match exactly. The score was 0.406 for AI Overviews and 0.377 for ChatGPT. Links marked as coming from user-generated content, such as forum posts, scored lower, at 0.342 and 0.314.

These are moderate relationships, and they don't show that links cause citations, since large, well-known sites tend to have more of everything. The samples also contain only domains cited at least once, so they can't tell you what it takes to get cited for the first time. A similar pattern shows up in ordinary rankings: domains ranking first had a median of 111 referring domains against 85 for positions 4 to 10, with heavy overlap between the groups. For AI Overviews, the median cited domain had 282 referring domains on the easiest keywords and 1,571 on the hardest, after the report excluded giant platforms like YouTube and Amazon and any domain with fewer than 50 referring domains. Small sites weren't measured at all. The ranges are also wide, at 518 to 5,765 for the middle half of domains on the hardest keywords, so sites with very different link profiles get cited.

Which page: cited pages often don't rank for the query

Ranking for a query and being cited for it are drifting apart. Ahrefs found 76% of pages cited in AI Overviews ranked in the top 10 for that query in July 2025, and about 38% in March 2026. The two studies differ in sample, parsing, and the Gemini model behind the Overviews, so the size of that fall isn't a clean measurement. One possible mechanism is what Google calls query fan-out: its documentation says these features may issue "multiple related searches across subtopics and data sources". A page could then be cited because it ranks for a related question the reader never typed. Ahrefs offers this only as a possibility, and its earlier study tested the idea and found that the data didn't support it.

The most careful test of page-level tactics we found is a study by the SEO software company SISTRIX, published in October 2026. It paired 48,527 pages cited by ChatGPT, AI Mode, or AI Overviews with uncited pages from the same site, which removes the site's overall strength from the comparison. In the table, a factor of 2.7 means pages with the feature were cited 2.7 times as often as pages without it.

Page featureFactorWhat SISTRIX says about it
Current year in the title2.7A rough stand-in for maintained content, not a title trick; an initial indication
Table of contents with jump links1.7Only 14% of pages had one; 2.5 on editorial sites
FAQ structured data1.5At 833 URLs it pointed the opposite way, a warning about small GEO studies
Visible last-updated date1.31.9 on editorial sites, but 0.7 on shops; only 5% of pages showed one
Ten or more external links1.3Linking out to sources
Product structured data0.80.5 in AI Overviews, but "not a lever, but no cause for concern either"; it should stay
Many features combined2.1Against barely optimized pages

An experiment in the paper that gave GEO its name points the same way as SISTRIX's correlations. Aggarwal and colleagues rewrote web pages and measured how much of a generated answer drew on them. On their 10,000-query benchmark, adding quotations raised a page's visibility by about 41%, adding statistics by about 31%, and citing sources by about 27%, while keyword stuffing lowered it by about 8%, all on their main measure, the position-weighted share of the answer's words. Lower-ranked pages gained the most: citing sources lifted a page ranked fifth by 115% and cut the top-ranked page by 30%. They also tried Perplexity, an AI search product, on 200 samples, uploading the source text as files rather than letting it search. The gains on that measure were smaller, at about 21% for quotations and 9% for statistics. The main test used GPT-3.5 reading the top five search results, which is well behind today's products, so the percentages are dated even if the direction still holds.

The most debated shortcut has nothing behind it so far. llms.txt is a proposed file that tells AI systems what a site contains. SE Ranking analyzed nearly 300,000 domains and found no correlation with citations. SISTRIX also concluded there is "no measurable effect", though it cautions that domains with the file differ from others in many ways, so this part of its data doesn't have the same-site pairing. Google says "you don't need to create new machine readable files, AI text files, or markup" for its AI features. The data agrees about the files, though SISTRIX's FAQ structured data result suggests some markup may help.

AI sends little traffic, but it is growing and may convert well

AI assistants sent 0.28% of total traffic across 74,752 websites in March 2026, according to Ahrefs. That was about 3.5 million visitors, against 345 million from Google, or roughly a hundred to one. Ahrefs describes it as small but growing fast. The true figure is somewhat higher because some visits, especially from mobile apps, get counted as direct traffic. The same Ahrefs article reports that on its own site, AI search visitors were 0.5% of visitors and 12.1% of signups. Ahrefs sells SEO software, so its audience may be unusually likely to use AI tools, and one site proves little. Still, on that site an AI visitor was about 24 times as likely to sign up as the average visitor. Some of the value never shows up as traffic. People read an AI answer, form an opinion, and never click.

To count what AI visits are worth on your own site, RevScope reports when ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and other assistants send visitors and whether they buy. It also tracks when AI and search engine bots crawl your pages.

Google's own reporting has a gap too. It counts traffic from its AI features inside the overall "Web" numbers in Search Console. Since 2026 Search Console also has generative AI reports, which Google says show how often your URLs appeared in those features, along with pages, countries, and devices. The announcement describes impressions and doesn't mention clicks, so you learn how often you appear, not how many visits or sales that brings. Rank tracking can't fill the gap, since a page can hold position 1 and earn fewer clicks than it used to.

What to do about it

  • Keep the fundamentals. Pages must be indexable and eligible for a snippet. Referring domains correlated with citations more strongly than user-generated links did, and higher-ranking domains had moderately more of them, so links from other sites remain a reasonable investment, even though neither relationship proves cause.
  • Find out who gets cited on your topics, per platform. Check your important queries in AI Overviews and ChatGPT and note the sources. Being described accurately there may matter as much as your own page. Take part in the communities those answers cite, such as Reddit, so that you are mentioned there.
  • Write pages worth quoting. Answer related questions directly, add original data and named sources, and use clear headings. If you run an editorial site, show when the page was last updated.
  • Skip the shortcuts. An llms.txt does no harm but has shown no benefit, AI-specific markup isn't needed, and keyword stuffing lowered visibility in the GEO paper's test.
  • Judge the work by revenue. With fewer clicks to go around, it matters more which ones pay. Tie each channel to the sales it produces rather than to its rank or its visit count.

The numbers above are mainly US English, and the products change quickly, so the 2025 figures may already be out of date. Nearly all the large datasets come from companies that sell SEO data or software, including DataForSEO, Ahrefs, SISTRIX, and SE Ranking, and we sell analytics. Almost everything about what earns a citation is correlation. Three findings hold up. Controlled experiments show fewer clicks to outside websites when Google's AI features are present, domains with more referring domains tend to be cited more often among those already cited, and we found no proven shortcut to being cited.

Stop guessing what makes money

RevScope connects your web traffic to your payments, so you can see which channels, pages, and keywords bring in revenue. Start on the free plan and put your time and budget where it pays.

Rather run it yourself? RevScope's source is public. Self-host it for free.

Sources

Search Insider: 2026 Edition
DataForSEO · Annual research report · October 2026
DataForSEO collects search and AI answer data for a living and publishes its tables and methods, which allowed us to check the monthly figures behind its headlines. It sells this data, its answer prompts aren't explained, and its click shares are modeled. We rely on it for what appears where, and treat its click estimates and correlations as indications. Our charts are redrawn from its published values.

The Impact of Google AI Overviews on Publisher Traffic and User Experience: Evidence from a Field Experiment
Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen · Working paper · SSRN · draft of June 2026
University researchers ran a preregistered randomized experiment on 1,065 US participants, 770 of them in the two groups compared here. Random assignment makes it the best evidence that Overviews themselves reduce clicks. It isn't yet peer reviewed, and it covers desktop Chrome for two weeks. We read a copy of the June draft hosted outside SSRN.

AI in Search Reduces Publisher Referrals Without Improving User Experience: Experimental Evidence
Stephanie T. Wang, Jeffrey Gleason, and colleagues · Preprint · arXiv · August 2026
A second preregistered experiment, with 1,100 people, which independently supports the direction of the result. We read its abstract only, so we use it for that direction and not for any figure.

Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears in the results
Athena Chapekis and Anna Lieb · Short read · Pew Research Center · July 2025
A nonprofit research organization with no search product to sell, logging the real browsing of 900 consenting US adults. It covers one month, March 2025, re-collected the summaries in April, and doesn't control for which searches draw a summary.

AI Features and Your Website and the Search Console reports announcement
Google Search Central · Documentation, last updated December 2025, and blog post, June 2026
The primary sources for what Google says its AI features require and how it reports them. They are reliable on those rules, and they aren't independent evidence of what works.

AI in Search is driving more queries and higher quality clicks
Liz Reid · Company blog · Google · August 2025
Google's public position on total clicks, from the person running Search. Google can see the true numbers, but this post publishes none of them, so we report it as a claim.

Citation Worthiness: Which GEO Tactics Hold Up Across 96,418 URLs
Johannes Beus, Julia Weissbach, and the SISTRIX Content Team · Industry study · SISTRIX · October 2026
Its same-site pairing and correction for multiple testing make it more careful than most GEO studies. It sells SEO software, covers only German-speaking markets, and reports correlations.

GEO: Generative Engine Optimization
Pranjal Aggarwal, Vishvak Murahari, and colleagues · Conference paper · KDD 2024 · version 3, June 2024
The academic paper that named the field and ran controlled rewrites of pages. It shows content changes can move visibility, but its test engine is now dated, and its authors' "up to 40%" should not be read as a current forecast.

Update: 38% of AI Overview Citations Pull From The Top 10 and 76% of AI Overview Citations Pull From the Top 10
Louise Linehan with Xibeijia Guan · Industry studies · Ahrefs · March 2026 and July 2025
Ahrefs sells SEO tools and tracks AI answers through its Brand Radar product, here matching about 4 million cited URLs against rankings in the later study. The two studies aren't like-for-like. The 38% counts results in every part of the page; for ordinary links alone it is 37.1%.

AI Chatbot Traffic: What It Is, and How to Get More
Mateusz Makosiewicz · Company blog · Ahrefs · May 2026
The source for the 0.28% figure, from analytics on 74,752 sites, and for the signup figure from Ahrefs' own site. It gives conflicting percentages for Google's share in different places, so we compare visitor counts instead.

LLMs.txt: Why Brands Rely On It and Why It Doesn't Work
Yulia Deda · Industry study · SE Ranking · page dated October 2026
A large correlation study of nearly 300,000 domains. It doesn't name the AI platforms it sampled, so we use it only alongside SISTRIX and Google's statement.

articles.title: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down
articles.full_content:
The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The NSA closed its campus to most employees on Tuesday night, reverting to essential personnel only as it works to restore the network, according to a voicemail inbox used by NSA employees and a source familiar with the matter.

The move to further restrict staffing levels came just hours after the NSA told employees they could return to work as normal. It is not clear what prompted the reversal. The agency had staggered employee arrivals earlier in the day as it worked to address the issue.

The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said.

“The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”

A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month.

“The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.”

The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. AI tools helped researchers exploit them, setting off a scramble by government agencies and corporations around the world to address the issue in recent weeks. The NSA itself urged organizations to apply software patches.

The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords.

Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack.

A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One.

Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. “It could impact analysis and reporting, but for highest priority requirements they would find a way to work those. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.”

A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a system of three main levels that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The recording told non-emergency personnel to arrive for work in a staggered manner and for emergency personnel to arrive as usual. The New York Times first reported that detail.

Sometime Tuesday evening, the inbox reverted to “code green,” instructing employees to report to work as scheduled. It was not immediately clear whether the outage was resolved. But later Tuesday night, the inbox moved to a “code orange,” closing the campus for most employees until further notice, according to the inbox recording and source familiar with the matter.

The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country.

All flights nationwide were grounded for hours on Friday after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas.

Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings.

And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts.

There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security.

The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official.

Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time.

This story has been updated with additional information.

Davis Winkie’s work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP). CNN retains full editorial control of the reporting.

CNN’s Kylie Atwood and Haley Britzky contributed reporting.

Title : Introduction

Author: Phrack Staff

View as text

|=-----------------------------------------------------------------------=| |=---------------------=[ Introduction ]=------------------------=| |=-----------------------------------------------------------------------=| |=---------------------=[ Phrack Staff ]=------------------------=| |=---------------------=[ [email protected] ]=------------------------=| |=-----------------------------------------------------------------------=| |=---------------------=[ September 30, 2026 ]=------------------------=| |=-----------------------------------------------------------------------=|

--[ Past ]

Last year marked the 40th anniversary of Phrack so we went big. We published
our anniversary launch release in print at Defcon 33, HOPE, WHY25 and some
additional variations at several conferences around the world including
AlligatorCon, B-Sides Canberra, Out of the Box, Datenspuren, DistrictCon,
OffensiveCon, Recon, and Toorcamp. We included a CTF with exploit challenges
and had puzzles and easter eggs included in the zine. We threw parties and
had talks at Defcon and WHY25 to celebrate this milestone.

More importantly, we got new research into people's hands. The point of the
relaunch was to get people reading, researching, writing, and contributing
again. We wanted the next person picking up Phrack to find something that
made them sit down at a computer and start pulling a system apart.

We owe a huge thanks to the authors, editors, artists, publishing partners,
donors, and staff who made it happen. Writing the paper, working through
revisions, putting the print editions together, paying the bills, and
getting boxes of zines to the right places all take time and effort. Most of
that work is invisible when you are holding the finished issue. We
appreciate everyone who did it.

And to the readers: thank you for giving a shit. Seeing someone get excited
about an article, connect it to something they are working on, or realize
that they could contribute something themselves makes the effort worthwhile.
That exchange is how this thing keeps going. The relaunch worked, and this
issue is the follow-through.

--[ Present ]

This is the third release curated by the new staff, and we are not slowing
down. This issue is larger than last year's, with 23 main papers and eight
additional articles in Line Noise. The subjects range from exploitation and
reverse engineering to machine learning, hardware, and the history and
culture that grew around this work.

We have container escapes through the vDSO, use-after-free exploitation, QNX
userland shellcode, Linux kernel research, and a Chromium renderer sandbox
escape through Skia. Elsewhere, the issue takes on Windows smart card
architecture, static taint analysis in Binary Ninja, and autonomous
underwater vehicles.  There is also work examining backdoors in machine
learning and what it means to trust an AI system. One paper takes us from
PhrackCTF to two WinFSP zero-days, which is a pretty good argument for
continuing to put challenges in a zine.

We also have four more articles in Phrack World History, including the story
of the infamous SSH1 CRC32 vulnerability featured in The Matrix Reloaded as
well as stories about blue boxing free phone calls, a confession of a hacker
who tried to backdoor Linux kernel in 2003, and an early discovery of
botnets for hire. Our Prophile features Halvar Flake, whose contributions to
reverse engineering and security research are legendary.

--[ Future ]

In 2026, we find ourselves in a time of rapid technological change. It is
hard to say what vulnerability research or red teaming will look like in
another five years. AI has moved well beyond completing a line of code into
agentic systems capable of analyzing source code and reverse engineering
binaries to find and exploit vulnerabilities.

We can be sure that the future will require us to continue to explore new
ideas, create new tools, and push the boundaries of what is possible in the
face of new challenges and opportunities created by the advancement of AI
and automation systems. As the effort required to put ideas into practice
falls, creativity and human intuition forged through experience is valued
even higher.

We hope that this release of Phrack will inspire new ideas, discussions, and
collaborations that will keep the human side of hacking a critical element
in shaping the future of technology and society. We will continue to do our
part to support the community and provide a platform for sharing knowledge
and ideas. We look forward to seeing what the future holds and we are
excited to be a part of it.

Read the papers, try the ideas, and challenge the conclusions. When you find
something worth sharing, write it up and send it in. We have another issue
to put together, and some of you should be in it!

--[ Greetz ]

To those who have supported us the past three years helping to restore
vitality to Phrack, we thank you.

Conferences who funded prints: Defcon, OffensiveCon, Recon, Unprompted[AU],
Unprompted[US], BSides Canberra, Alligatorcon, TenguCon

Sponsors & Major Donors - WatchTowr, Elltam, Verichains, BShield,
TrustedSec, Binarly, Trenchant, Praetorian (WWSUL), EFF, Blaze, EMX,
Mullvad, ToorCon, Hacker Initiative, Endrazine, Dug Song, Napster, halvar,
Horizon, Huku, Julio Auto, Gadi, and the rest of the people who stepped up with
smaller donations.

Artists - Ian Dash, pinguino, tainted, pepper, mar, xer0, abstrakt, ToscaKaiser,
h7, zir, Mick, p0rtL, netspooky, ackmage, digitalis, Tedsig42, and the many
others who submitted their work for consideration.

Reviewers - barbie, bsdaemon, C, chompie, danielcuthbert, devinc, grugq, joern,
jordan9001, K3, richinseattle, roddux, saber, skyper, SSHad0w, TMZ, zh4ck

All the authors past and present who are now bound to the history of phrack.

The unnamed ones who have helped us with logistics and carrying literal tons
of paper around conferences to deliver them into the hands of the next
generation.

--[ Disclaimer ]

All information in Phrack Magazine is, to the best of the ability of
the editors and contributors, truthful and accurate. When possible,
all facts are checked, all code is compiled. However, we are not
omniscient (hell, we don’t even get paid). It is entirely possible
something contained within this publication is incorrect in some way.
If this is the case, please drop us some email so that we can correct
it in a future issue.

Also, keep in mind that Phrack Magazine accepts no responsibility for
the entirely stupid (or illegal) things people may do with the
